1.translation: Arjuna said: Those devotees who, always disciplined in this way, worship you, and those who instead worship the imperishable and unmanifest — which of them know yoga best?
1.nuances: Sivananda, Sankaranarayan and Adidevananda keep the neutral 'worship/meditate' and 'best knowers of Yoga', while Purohit recasts the question as Personal God versus Impersonal and Prabhupada frames it as 'devotional service' versus 'impersonal Brahman'. Gambirananda alone glosses yoga here as samadhi, and Sankaranarayan renders avyakta as 'motionless Unmanifest'.

2.translation: The Blessed Lord said: Those who fix their mind on me and worship me with constant discipline, endowed with the highest faith — these I consider the most perfectly united in yoga.
2.nuances: All agree the verse ranks the devotees of the personal Lord highest; they differ on yuktatama, rendered 'best in Yoga' (Sivananda), 'the very best' (Purohit), 'most perfect yogis' (Gambirananda, Prabhupada) or 'best among the masters of Yoga' (Sankaranarayan). Prabhupada adds 'My personal form' and 'transcendental faith', making the devotional reading explicit.

3.translation: But those who worship the imperishable, the indefinable, the unmanifest, the all-pervading and inconceivable, the unchanging, immovable and eternal,
3.nuances: Only Prabhupada is given, and his text is actually his rendering of verse 5 (the 'greater difficulty' of the impersonalists), so the source data does not contain any direct rendering of this list of epithets for the Absolute.

4.translation: having fully restrained the whole group of senses, even-minded in every circumstance and delighting in the welfare of all beings — they too reach none other than me.
4.nuances: Sivananda, Adidevananda and Gambirananda stress 'they too / Me alone', keeping the point that impersonal worshippers also reach the Lord; Sankaranarayan is most literal ('group of sense-organs', 'find pleasure in the welfare'). Prabhupada's entry is misaligned and actually corresponds to 9.22 ('I provide what they lack'), so it does not render this verse.

5.translation: The toil is greater for those whose minds cling to the unmanifest, for the unmanifest goal is reached only with difficulty by embodied beings.
5.nuances: Sivananda, Gambirananda, Adidevananda and Sankaranarayan all render kleśa as 'trouble/struggle/difficulty' and keep gati as the 'goal' or 'way'. Purohit adds the gloss that the embodied find it hard to realise the Lord 'as without one', and Prabhupada turns gati into 'advancement' or 'progress' in a 'discipline'.

6.translation: But those who surrender all their actions to me, hold me as their highest aim, and worship me, meditating on me with a yoga that admits nothing else —
6.nuances: All treat this as the first half of a sentence completed in verse 7. The key phrase ananyena yogena becomes 'single-minded Yoga' (Sivananda), 'no thought save of Me' (Purohit), 'exclusive devotion' (Adidevananda) or, very literally, a Yoga 'which admits no other element but Me' (Sankaranarayan); Prabhupada merges verses 6 and 7 into one devotional statement.

7.translation: for them, Pārtha, whose thoughts have entered into me, I soon become the one who lifts them out of the ocean of death-bound existence.
7.nuances: Translators differ on mṛtyusaṃsārasāgara: 'ocean of Samsara' (Sivananda), 'ocean of life and death' (Purohit, Prabhupada), 'sea of the world which is fraught with death' (Gambirananda), 'ocean of mortal life' (Adidevananda), 'ocean of the death-cycle' (Sankaranarayan). Purohit and Sivananda drop the epithet in favour of 'Arjuna', while the rest keep 'son of Pṛthā'.

8.translation: Set your mind on me alone and let your understanding enter into me; from then on you will dwell in me alone, there is no doubt of it.
8.nuances: Most render buddhi as 'intellect' or 'reason', Adidevananda leaves it untranslated as 'Buddhi'. Sankaranarayan reads ata ūrdhvam not as 'hereafter' but as 'resorting to the best Yoga', an unusual construal; Prabhupada inserts 'the Supreme Personality of Godhead' after 'Me'.

9.translation: But if you cannot hold your mind steadily fixed on me, then seek to reach me by the yoga of repeated practice, Dhanañjaya.
9.nuances: Abhyāsa-yoga is 'Yoga of constant practice' (Sivananda), 'constant practice' (Purohit), 'Yoga of Practice' (Gambirananda), 'practice of repetition' (Adidevananda) and 'practice-Yoga' (Sankaranarayan); Prabhupada alone identifies it with 'the regulative principles of bhakti-yoga'. Purohit replaces the epithet with 'My beloved friend'.

10.translation: If you are unable even to practise, then make action done for my sake your highest aim; even by performing works for me you will attain perfection.
10.nuances: Gambirananda glosses siddhi as identity with Brahman, whereas Purohit and Prabhupada read it as 'the goal' or 'the perfect stage' of devotion. Adidevananda explicitly glosses matkarma as 'service', and Purohit similarly says 'devote thyself to My service'.

11.translation: And if you cannot do even this, then take refuge in union with me and, with your self under control, renounce the fruits of all your actions.
11.nuances: Madyogam āśritaḥ is read as 'resorting to union with Me' (Sivananda, Purohit), 'the Yoga for Me' (Gambirananda) or 'My Yoga' (Adidevananda, Sankaranarayan); Prabhupada paraphrases it as 'work in this consciousness of Me'. Yatātmavān is rendered 'self-controlled' by all except Prabhupada's 'self-situated'.

12.translation: Knowledge is indeed better than practice, and meditation surpasses knowledge; better than meditation is the renunciation of the fruits of action, and from renunciation peace follows at once.
12.nuances: Sivananda, Gambirananda and Adidevananda read a simple ascending series ending in renunciation; Sankaranarayan instead reads each as the source of the next ('because of knowledge, meditation becomes pre-eminent'). Purohit replaces 'practice' with 'blind action', and Prabhupada adds a conditional opening ('If you cannot take to this practice') to fit his scheme of graded alternatives.

13.translation: One who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free from possessiveness and from the sense of 'I', the same in sorrow and in joy, and patient,
13.nuances: Nirmama and nirahaṅkāra are rendered 'free from attachment and egoism' (Sivananda), 'free from selfishness, without pride' (Purohit) or the more literal 'free from the sense of mine and I' (Gambirananda, Adidevananda, Sankaranarayan). Kṣamī is 'forgiving' for most, 'enduring' for Adidevananda and 'forbearance' for Sankaranarayan; Prabhupada's entry is misaligned and actually renders verse 6.

14.translation: always content, a yogin, self-controlled and firm in resolve, with mind and understanding offered to me — such a devotee of mine is dear to me.
14.nuances: Yogī is kept as 'a yogi' or 'man of Yoga' by Gambirananda and Sankaranarayan, but interpreted as 'steady in meditation' (Sivananda), 'self-centred' (Purohit) or 'ever meditates' (Adidevananda). Prabhupada's entry is misaligned and belongs to verse 7.

15.translation: One from whom the world does not shrink and who does not shrink from the world, who is free from elation, impatience, fear and anxiety — that one too is dear to me.
15.nuances: Udvijate is 'agitated' (Sivananda, Sankaranarayan), 'disturbed' (Gambirananda), 'frightened' (Adidevananda) or 'harmed' (Purohit); Prabhupada reads it as 'put into difficulty'. Amarṣa is 'anger' for Sivananda and Purohit but 'impatience' for Gambirananda, Adidevananda and Sankaranarayan, and Prabhupada replaces the four-item list with 'equipoised in happiness and distress'.

16.translation: One who expects nothing, who is pure, capable and impartial, untroubled, who has given up all personal undertakings — such a devotee of mine is dear to me.
16.nuances: Dakṣa is 'expert' (Sivananda, Adidevananda, Prabhupada), 'dextrous' (Gambirananda, Sankaranarayan) or 'watchful' (Purohit); udāsīna ranges from 'unconcerned' to 'indifferent' and 'impartial'. Prabhupada paraphrases sarvārambhaparityāgī as 'not striving for some result' and anapekṣa as 'not dependent on the ordinary course of activities', softening the sense of renouncing undertakings.

17.translation: One who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor craves, who has let go of both good and bad and is full of devotion — that one is dear to me.
17.nuances: All agree on the four negations; they differ on śubhāśubha, taken as 'good and evil' (Sivananda, Adidevananda), 'good and evil fortunes' (Purohit), 'good and bad results of actions' (Sankaranarayan) or 'auspicious and inauspicious things' (Prabhupada). Gambirananda renders dveṣṭi as 'fret' rather than 'hate'.

18.translation: Alike toward enemy and friend, alike in honour and dishonour, alike in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and free from attachment,
18.nuances: Only Prabhupada renders this verse, treating it together with verse 19 and adding 'remains steady in situations of gain or loss', which is not in the Sanskrit of this verse.

19.translation: equal to blame and praise, silent, content with whatever comes, without a fixed home, steady in mind and full of devotion — such a person is dear to me.
19.nuances: Aniketa is 'homeless' (Sivananda, Gambirananda), 'no fixed abode' (Purohit), 'no home' (Adidevananda), but Sankaranarayan reads it metaphorically as 'no fixed thought in the mundane life'. Maunī is 'silent' for most, with Purohit's 'enjoys silence'; Prabhupada's entry is the second half of his combined 18-19 and replaces 'homeless' with 'free from possessiveness'.

20.translation: But those who honour this immortal teaching of dharma just as it has been declared, full of faith and holding me as their highest — those devotees are exceedingly dear to me.
20.nuances: Dharmyāmṛtam is the crux: 'immortal Dharma' (Sivananda), 'spiritual wisdom' (Purohit), 'ambrosia indistinguishable from the virtues' (Gambirananda, with a note on the variant dharmāmṛtam), 'nectar of virtuous-duty' (Adidevananda), 'duty conducive to immortality' (Sankaranarayan) and 'imperishable path of devotional service' (Prabhupada). Gambirananda alone comments that 'tu' marks off the perfected devotees from the aspirants.

21.translation: Oṁ, that is the real. Thus ends the twelfth chapter, called the Yoga of Devotion, in the Upaniṣads of the glorious Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna.
